title: Ang 1232–1236: Sarang ashtpadis

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ninth: whose mother, whose father? Love your people, and know they aren't the last helper. A short hymn, and a hard one. Today the hymns get longer.
screen: `THE NINTH: WHOSE MOTHER, WHOSE FATHER?` → `NOW, LONGER HYMNS.`

segments.voice: Some things fit in a text. Some need a voice memo that runs eleven minutes, where you keep circling back to the one thing you actually called to say. On ang 1232, Sarang changes its heading to asatpadeeaa: longer hymns. Same raga, same Gurus, more stanzas. So why would a Guru need the longer form?
screen: `A TEXT, OR AN ELEVEN-MINUTE MEMO.` → `ASATPADEEAA: LONGER HYMNS.` → `WHY THE LONGER FORM?`

segments.voice: Because some things need walking around. A short hymn says it and stops. A longer one takes one longing and turns it, stanza by stanza, like walking all the way around a tree to see it whole. And it doesn't get lost, because it still has a rahau, the pause line, the center every stanza leans back toward. Something to tell a friend tonight: in kirtan, the singers return to the rahau between stanzas, so even a listener who loses the thread gets handed the center again. One of these Sarang hymns, in paraphrase, opens: without the Lord, how can I live, my mother? Then it spends its length on that one question. That's the two weeks behind us, too, if you walk around them: nothing outside the One; one clay; serve the One; the Name not knotted; the milk; what's seen will pass; forever spring; Ramanand, colored at home; the Name running cool at noon. Many stanzas, one center.
screen: `SOME THINGS NEED WALKING AROUND.` · `THE RAHAU: THE CENTER.` · `HOW CAN I LIVE WITHOUT YOU?` · `TWO WEEKS, ONE CENTER.` · then, large: `LONGER HYMNS.`

segments.voice: Take a scrap of paper and write, by hand, the one line from these two weeks you'd want to keep. Just one. Then sit with it in front of you, your rahau, and let the other lines circle it. If you'd like, read ang 1232 before you begin.
Ang 1232. Where Sarang's longer hymns begin, many stanzas around one center.
Longer hymns: when one thing matters enough, you walk all the way around it, and keep coming back. That's the fortnight.

notes: 2026-10-15 v3 written: shape review (the asatpadeeaa taught lightly; the fortnight's carries come back in the recall, the match and the teach).

Confirm that a Sarang asatpadi within ang 1232–1236 opens 'har bin kio jeevaa meree maaee' (writer's recollection: Mahala 1, near ang 1232); paraphrased and not attributed to a specific Guru in the voice for that reason.
The script avoids any claim about the word asatpadeeaa's origin or a fixed number of stanzas; it says only 'longer hymns' and 'more stanzas'.
The trapdoor's 'shorter hymns first, then asatpadeeaa, then longer forms' describes the usual order within a raga; confirm wording.

v3 storyline close (Simran, days 1583–1596): the gurmat camp ends with the closing program; the kids forget verses but sing every rahau, and Simran cries.
